items.name: Egbert
facts: Became King of Wessex in 802 after years in exile at the court of Charlemagne.
Defeated the Mercians at the Battle of Ellendun in 825 and took Kent, Surrey, Sussex and Essex.
In 829 he briefly ruled Mercia too, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle calls him a Bretwalda, or overlord of Britain.
Defeated a joint Viking and Cornish army at Hingston Down in 838.
Died in 839 and was succeeded by his son Æthelwulf.

items.name: Æthelwulf
facts: Son of Egbert; he had ruled Kent for his father before becoming King of Wessex in 839.
Won a major victory over a Viking army at the Battle of Aclea in 851.
Went on pilgrimage to Rome in 855, taking his youngest son Alfred with him.
Married Judith, daughter of the Frankish king Charles the Bald, in 856.
On his return his son Æthelbald refused to give up power, so the kingdom was shared between them.
Father of four kings in turn: Æthelbald, Æthelberht, Æthelred I and Alfred the Great.
Died in 858.

items.name: Æthelbald
facts: Eldest surviving son of Æthelwulf.
Rebelled against his father in 855 while Æthelwulf was away in Rome.
Married his father's young widow Judith, which shocked the Church.
Died in 860 after a short reign and was buried at Sherborne.

items.name: Æthelberht
facts: Brother of Æthelbald; he had ruled Kent before 860.
Ruled Wessex and Kent together as one kingdom, instead of dividing them as before.
Vikings sacked Winchester, the royal city, during his reign.
Died in 865 and was buried at Sherborne, succeeded by his brother Æthelred.

items.name: Æthelred I
facts: Fourth son of Æthelwulf; brother of Æthelberht and of Alfred.
The Great Heathen Army of Danes landed in East Anglia in 865, the year he became king.
Fought the Danes with his brother Alfred in several battles in 870 and 871.
Won the Battle of Ashdown in January 871, but lost other battles that year.
Died in April 871, and his brother Alfred succeeded him because his own sons were children.
Buried at Wimborne Minster in Dorset.

items.name: Alfred the Great
facts: Youngest son of Æthelwulf; became king in 871 when his brother Æthelred I died.
Driven into hiding in the marshes of Athelney, Somerset, by a Danish surprise attack in early 878.
The famous story of Alfred burning the cakes comes from his time hiding at Athelney.
Defeated the Danish leader Guthrum at the Battle of Edington in May 878.
Guthrum was baptised, and a treaty divided England, with the Danes keeping the Danelaw.
Built a network of fortified towns called burhs and reorganised the army and navy.
Loved learning, translated Latin books into English, and issued a law code.
The only English king called 'the Great'; died 26 October 899.

items.name: Edward the Elder
facts: Son of Alfred the Great.
His cousin Æthelwold rebelled with Danish help, but was killed at the Battle of the Holme in 902.
With his sister Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, he conquered the Danish Midlands and East Anglia.
By 918 he ruled all England south of the Humber.
Took direct control of Mercia when Æthelflæd died in 918.
Died at Farndon in Cheshire in 924 and was succeeded by his son Æthelstan.

items.name: Æthelstan
facts: Son of Edward the Elder; brought up in Mercia.
Took York from the Vikings in 927, so he is often called the first King of all England.
Won the great Battle of Brunanburh in 937 against the Scots, the Strathclyde Britons and the Dublin Vikings.
Issued many law codes and collected holy relics.
Married his half-sisters to rulers across Europe.
Never married and had no children; succeeded by his half-brother Edmund.
Died at Gloucester in 939 and was buried at Malmesbury Abbey.

items.name: Edmund I
facts: Half-brother of Æthelstan; became king aged 18.
Fought alongside Æthelstan at Brunanburh in 937 as a teenager.
Lost the north to the Vikings in 939 but recovered the Five Boroughs in 942 and York in 944.
Invaded Strathclyde in 945 and handed it to King Malcolm I of Scotland as an ally.
Supported Dunstan and made him Abbot of Glastonbury.
Stabbed to death at a feast at Pucklechurch, Gloucestershire, on 26 May 946 by a robber named Leofa.
Succeeded by his brother Eadred, because his sons Eadwig and Edgar were small children.

items.name: Eadred
facts: Younger brother of Edmund I and son of Edward the Elder.
Fought the Viking king Eric Bloodaxe for control of York.
Eric Bloodaxe was driven out and killed in 954, ending the Viking kingdom of York.
Suffered from a long illness and could only swallow the juices of his food.
Relied heavily on Dunstan and on his mother Eadgifu.
Died at Frome on 23 November 955, unmarried, and was succeeded by his nephew Eadwig.

items.name: Eadwig
facts: Eldest son of Edmund I; became king aged about 15.
The story goes that he left his coronation feast to be with a young woman, Ælfgifu, and her mother.
Dunstan dragged him back to the feast, and Eadwig sent Dunstan into exile.
He married Ælfgifu, but Archbishop Oda annulled the marriage in 958 because they were too closely related.
In 957 the Mercians and Northumbrians chose his brother Edgar as their king, splitting the kingdom at the Thames.
Died on 1 October 959, aged about 19, and Edgar reunited the kingdom.

items.name: Edgar the Peaceful
facts: Younger son of Edmund I; king north of the Thames from 957 and of all England from 959.
His reign was free of Viking attacks, which is why he is called 'the Peaceful'.
Backed the monastic reform led by Dunstan, Æthelwold and Oswald, making Dunstan Archbishop of Canterbury.
Crowned at Bath in 973 in a ceremony that became the model for later English coronations.
After the coronation, several British kings rowed him along the River Dee at Chester as a sign of submission.
Reformed the coinage in about 973 so that the whole kingdom used one standard currency.
Father of Edward the Martyr and Æthelred the Unready by different wives.
Died on 8 July 975, aged only about 32.

items.name: Edward the Martyr
facts: Eldest son of Edgar; his succession was disputed by supporters of his young half-brother Æthelred.
Dunstan backed Edward, but his short reign saw a backlash against the reformed monasteries.
Murdered at Corfe in Dorset on 18 March 978 while visiting his stepmother Ælfthryth and Æthelred.
Later writers blamed Ælfthryth, Æthelred's mother, for the killing.
Miracles were reported at his tomb; his body was moved to Shaftesbury Abbey in 979 and he became a saint.

items.name: Æthelred the Unready
facts: Son of Edgar and Ælfthryth; became king aged about 10 after the murder of his half-brother Edward.
'Unready' comes from Old English 'unræd', meaning 'bad counsel', a pun on his name, which means 'noble counsel'.
Viking raids began again; the English were beaten at the Battle of Maldon in 991, remembered in a famous poem.
Paid huge sums of Danegeld to buy off the Vikings, starting with 10,000 pounds in 991.
Married Emma of Normandy in 1002; she was the mother of Edward the Confessor.
Ordered the St Brice's Day massacre of Danes living in England on 13 November 1002.
Sweyn Forkbeard of Denmark invaded in 1013, and Æthelred fled to Normandy.

items.name: Sweyn Forkbeard
facts: King of Denmark from about 986, after rebelling against his father Harald Bluetooth.
Raided England repeatedly from 1003, after the St Brice's Day massacre.
Invaded in 1013; by Christmas the English had accepted him as king and Æthelred had fled to Normandy.
Died at Gainsborough, Lincolnshire, on 3 February 1014, after only about five weeks as king.
Never crowned; the shortest reign of any King of England.
Father of Cnut the Great and grandfather of Harold Harefoot and Harthacnut.

items.name: Æthelred the Unready
facts: Recalled from Normandy by the Witan in 1014 after Sweyn's death, on condition that he governed better.
This is the first known agreement between an English king and his subjects.
Drove Sweyn's son Cnut out of England in 1014.
Cnut returned with a large fleet in 1015, and Æthelred's son Edmund Ironside led the resistance.
Died in London on 23 April 1016.
Reigned about 37 years in total, the longest of any Anglo-Saxon king.

items.name: Edmund Ironside
facts: Son of Æthelred the Unready by his first wife.
Nicknamed 'Ironside' for his bravery and toughness in fighting Cnut.
Chosen as king by the people of London in April 1016, while other nobles chose Cnut.
Fought Cnut in a string of battles in 1016, including Penselwood, Sherston, Brentford and Otford.
Defeated at Assandun in Essex on 18 October 1016 after the ealdorman Eadric Streona changed sides.
Agreed with Cnut to divide England: Edmund kept Wessex and Cnut took the north.
Died on 30 November 1016, possibly murdered, and Cnut took the whole kingdom.
Grandfather of Edgar Ætheling through his son Edward the Exile.

items.name: Cnut the Great
facts: Son of Sweyn Forkbeard; became king of all England after Edmund Ironside died in 1016.
Also King of Denmark from 1018 and of Norway from 1028, ruling a North Sea empire.
Married Emma of Normandy, Æthelred's widow, in 1017.
Had the treacherous Eadric Streona executed in 1017.
Divided England into four great earldoms: Wessex, Mercia, East Anglia and Northumbria.
Paid off his fleet in 1018 with a tax of 82,500 pounds, the largest Danegeld ever raised.
The famous story says he had his throne put by the sea to show his courtiers that even a king cannot stop the tide.
A generous supporter of the Church; he travelled to Rome in 1027 for the Emperor's coronation.
Died at Shaftesbury on 12 November 1035 and was buried at Winchester.

items.name: Harold Harefoot
facts: Son of Cnut by his first wife, Ælfgifu of Northampton.
His nickname probably refers to his speed and skill as a hunter.
Became regent in 1035 because his half-brother Harthacnut was busy in Denmark, then king in 1037.
In 1036 Æthelred's son Alfred came to England, was seized and blinded, and died; Earl Godwin was blamed.
Sent Queen Emma into exile in Flanders in 1037.
Died at Oxford on 17 March 1040 and was buried at Westminster.
Harthacnut later had his body dug up and thrown into a marsh.

items.name: Harthacnut
facts: Son of Cnut and Emma of Normandy; King of Denmark from 1035.
Was preparing to invade England when Harold Harefoot died, and was invited to take the throne in 1040.
Had Harold's body dug up, beheaded and thrown into the Thames.
Raised a very heavy tax to pay for his fleet; when Worcester rebelled he had the town burned in 1041.
In 1041 invited his half-brother Edward, later the Confessor, back from Normandy to share his court.
Collapsed while drinking at a wedding feast at Lambeth and died on 8 June 1042.
The last Danish king of England.

items.name: Edward the Confessor
facts: Son of Æthelred the Unready and Emma of Normandy; spent about 25 years in exile in Normandy.
Became king in 1042 when his half-brother Harthacnut died; crowned at Winchester at Easter 1043.
Married Edith, daughter of Earl Godwin, in 1045, but they had no children.
Quarrelled with Godwin and exiled him in 1051, but Godwin returned in force in 1052.
Rebuilt Westminster Abbey, which was consecrated on 28 December 1065, a week before he died.
Called 'the Confessor' because of his piety; made a saint in 1161.
Died on 5 January 1066 and was buried in his new abbey; Harold Godwinson was chosen to succeed him.
Patron saint of England until Edward III promoted St George.

items.name: Harold II
facts: Son of Earl Godwin; Earl of Wessex from 1053 and the most powerful man in England.
Norman writers say he swore an oath in Normandy, about 1064, to support William's claim to the throne.
Crowned on 6 January 1066, the day after Edward the Confessor died.
Defeated the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada and his own brother Tostig at Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066.
Marched south and was killed at the Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066.
The Bayeux Tapestry seems to show him struck in the eye by an arrow.
The last Anglo-Saxon king of England; he reigned about nine months.

items.name: Edgar Ætheling
facts: Grandson of Edmund Ironside; his father Edward the Exile died in 1057 soon after returning to England.
Chosen as king by the Witan in London after Hastings in October 1066, aged about 15.
Submitted to William at Berkhamsted in December 1066 and was never crowned.
Joined rebellions against William in the north in 1069 and later took refuge in Scotland.
His sister Margaret married Malcolm III of Scotland and became St Margaret.
Went on the First Crusade and lived on quietly into the 1120s.

items.name: William I (the Conqueror)
facts: Duke of Normandy from 1035, aged about seven; the illegitimate son of Duke Robert, so also called 'the Bastard'.
Claimed that Edward the Confessor had promised him the English throne.
Defeated and killed Harold at the Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066.
Crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066.
Crushed rebellion in the north with the brutal Harrying of the North in 1069 and 1070.
Built castles across England, including the White Tower at the Tower of London.
Ordered the Domesday Book survey of England in 1085; it was completed in 1086.
Died at Rouen on 9 September 1087 after a riding injury, and was buried at Caen.
Left Normandy to his eldest son Robert and England to his son William Rufus.

items.name: William II (Rufus)
facts: Third son of William the Conqueror; called 'Rufus' for his red face or red hair.
Fought his elder brother Robert Curthose for Normandy; Robert pawned the duchy to him in 1096 to go on crusade.
Quarrelled with Archbishop Anselm, who went into exile in 1097.
Built Westminster Hall, finished in 1099.
Never married and had no children.
Killed by an arrow while hunting in the New Forest on 2 August 1100; Walter Tirel was blamed.
His younger brother Henry seized the treasury at Winchester and was crowned three days later.
The Rufus Stone in the New Forest marks the spot where he is said to have fallen.

items.name: Henry I
facts: Youngest son of William the Conqueror; nicknamed 'Beauclerc' for his learning.
Seized the throne in 1100 when William Rufus died, while his brother Robert was away on crusade.
Issued a Charter of Liberties at his coronation, later used as a model for Magna Carta.
Married Edith (renamed Matilda) of Scotland, a descendant of Alfred, in 1100.
Defeated Robert at Tinchebrai in 1106, took Normandy, and kept Robert in prison for 28 years.
His only legitimate son, William, drowned in the White Ship disaster on 25 November 1120.
Made his barons swear to accept his daughter Matilda as heir in 1127.
Fathered more than 20 illegitimate children, a record for an English king.
Died in Normandy on 1 December 1135, supposedly after eating too many lampreys.

items.name: Stephen
facts: Grandson of William the Conqueror through his daughter Adela; nephew of Henry I.
Rushed to England when Henry died and was crowned in December 1135, despite his oath to Matilda.
His reign became a civil war with Matilda known as 'the Anarchy'.
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle said of these years that 'Christ and his saints slept'.
Captured at the Battle of Lincoln on 2 February 1141 and later exchanged for Matilda's half-brother Robert of Gloucester.
His son Eustace died in 1153, and the Treaty of Wallingford let Stephen keep the throne for life.
Agreed that Matilda's son Henry of Anjou would succeed him.
Died at Dover on 25 October 1154 and was buried at Faversham Abbey.

items.name: Empress Matilda
facts: Daughter of Henry I; called 'Empress' from her first marriage to the Holy Roman Emperor Henry V.
Her second husband was Geoffrey Plantagenet, Count of Anjou; their son became Henry II.
Henry I named her his heir and made the barons swear to support her in 1127.
Landed in England in 1139 to fight Stephen, backed by her half-brother Robert of Gloucester.
After Stephen's capture in 1141 she was declared 'Lady of the English', but London drove her out before her coronation.
Escaped from besieged Oxford Castle across the snow, wrapped in a white cloak, in December 1142.
Left England in 1148 and died in Normandy in 1167.

items.name: Henry II
facts: Son of Empress Matilda and Geoffrey of Anjou; the first Plantagenet king.
The name Plantagenet comes from the sprig of broom, 'planta genista', that Geoffrey wore.
Married Eleanor of Aquitaine in 1152, so he ruled England, Normandy, Anjou and Aquitaine: the Angevin Empire.
Reformed the law with travelling royal judges and juries; seen as the founder of English common law.
Quarrelled with Archbishop Thomas Becket, his former chancellor, over the rights of the Church.
Four of his knights murdered Becket in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170.
Did public penance at Becket's tomb in 1174.
His sons rebelled against him in 1173 and 1174, backed by Queen Eleanor.
Died at Chinon on 6 July 1189, after learning that his favourite son John had joined Richard's rebellion.

items.name: Richard I (the Lionheart)
facts: Third son of Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine; became king in 1189.
Spent only about six months of his ten-year reign in England.
Led the Third Crusade from 1190; captured Acre in 1191 and beat Saladin at Arsuf.
Failed to retake Jerusalem but agreed a truce with Saladin in 1192.
Captured on his way home by Leopold of Austria and held for ransom by the Emperor Henry VI.
England paid a ransom of 150,000 marks to free him in 1194.
His brother John plotted against him while he was away, but Richard forgave him.
Hit by a crossbow bolt at the siege of Châlus and died on 6 April 1199.
Had no legitimate children; succeeded by his brother John.

items.name: John
facts: Youngest son of Henry II; nicknamed 'Lackland' because he was given no lands as a boy.
Became king in 1199, pushing aside his nephew Arthur of Brittany, who vanished in 1203.
Lost Normandy, Anjou and most of his French lands to Philip II of France by 1204.
Quarrelled with the Pope over the choice of archbishop; England was placed under interdict in 1208.
Excommunicated in 1209, but made peace with the Pope in 1213.
His allies were crushed by Philip II at Bouvines in 1214, ending his hopes of recovering Normandy.
Forced by rebel barons to seal Magna Carta at Runnymede on 15 June 1215.
Lost his baggage train and treasure crossing the Wash in October 1216.
Died of dysentery at Newark Castle on 18 October 1216 and was buried in Worcester Cathedral.

items.name: Henry III
facts: Son of John; became king aged nine in 1216, with William Marshal as regent.
Magna Carta was reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225; the 1225 version became the final text.
Reigned for 56 years, the longest reign of any medieval English king.
Rebuilt Westminster Abbey in the Gothic style from 1245 as a shrine to Edward the Confessor.
Married Eleanor of Provence in 1236; her foreign relatives were deeply unpopular.
Barons led by Simon de Montfort forced the Provisions of Oxford on him in 1258.
Defeated and captured by de Montfort at the Battle of Lewes on 14 May 1264.
De Montfort's parliament of 1265 was the first to include knights and townsmen together.
His son Edward defeated and killed de Montfort at Evesham on 4 August 1265.
Died on 16 November 1272 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.

items.name: Edward I
facts: Son of Henry III; called 'Longshanks' for his height and 'Hammer of the Scots'.
Was on crusade when his father died; crowned in 1274.
Conquered Wales between 1277 and 1283; Prince Llywelyn was killed in 1282.
Built the great Welsh castles of Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech and Beaumaris.
Made his son the first English Prince of Wales in 1301.
Expelled all Jews from England in 1290.
Built the Eleanor Crosses in memory of his wife Eleanor of Castile, who died in 1290.
Invaded Scotland in 1296 and took the Stone of Scone to Westminster.
Defeated William Wallace at Falkirk in 1298; Wallace was executed in 1305.
Died on 7 July 1307 at Burgh by Sands while marching against Robert the Bruce.

items.name: Edward II
facts: Son of Edward I; the first English Prince of Wales.
Devoted to his favourite Piers Gaveston, whom angry barons killed in 1312.
Married Isabella of France in 1308.
Heavily defeated by Robert the Bruce at Bannockburn on 23 and 24 June 1314.
Later relied on the hated Despensers, Hugh the father and Hugh the son.
Beat the rebel barons at Boroughbridge in 1322 and executed his cousin Thomas of Lancaster.
His wife Isabella and her lover Roger Mortimer invaded in 1326 and overthrew him.
Forced to give up the throne in January 1327 in favour of his son Edward III.
Died at Berkeley Castle in September 1327, almost certainly murdered.

items.name: Edward III
facts: Son of Edward II; became king aged 14 when his father was deposed in 1327.
Took real power in 1330, executing Roger Mortimer and sidelining his mother Isabella.
Claimed the French throne through his mother, starting the Hundred Years' War in 1337.
Won the sea battle of Sluys in 1340 and the Battle of Crécy on 26 August 1346.
Captured Calais in 1347 after a long siege.
His son, the Black Prince, won at Poitiers in 1356 and captured the French king.
Founded the Order of the Garter in about 1348.
The Black Death reached England in 1348 and killed perhaps a third of the people.
Parliament split into Lords and Commons during his reign, and English replaced French in the law courts in 1362.
The Black Prince died in 1376; Edward died on 21 June 1377 and was succeeded by his grandson Richard II.

items.name: Richard II
facts: Son of the Black Prince and grandson of Edward III; became king aged 10.
Faced the Peasants' Revolt in 1381, meeting the rebel leader Wat Tyler at Smithfield aged 14.
The Lords Appellant seized control and the Merciless Parliament of 1388 executed his friends.
Took revenge on the Appellants in 1397, executing or exiling them.
A great patron of art: the Wilton Diptych and the hammerbeam roof of Westminster Hall date from his reign.
Married Anne of Bohemia in 1382 and, after her death, the child princess Isabella of France in 1396.
Exiled his cousin Henry Bolingbroke in 1398 and seized the Lancaster estates when John of Gaunt died in 1399.
Bolingbroke invaded while Richard was in Ireland and Richard was deposed in September 1399.
Died in Pontefract Castle in February 1400, probably starved to death.

items.name: Henry IV
facts: Son of John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, a younger son of Edward III.
Known as Henry Bolingbroke, after the castle in Lincolnshire where he was born.
Exiled by Richard II in 1398; returned in 1399, deposed Richard and took the throne.
Faced the long Welsh revolt of Owain Glyndwr, which began in 1400.
Defeated the rebel Percy family at Shrewsbury on 21 July 1403; Harry Hotspur was killed.
Had Archbishop Scrope of York executed for rebellion in 1405.
A law of 1401 allowed heretics, the Lollards, to be burned at the stake.
Suffered from a disfiguring skin disease in his last years.
Died on 20 March 1413 in the Jerusalem Chamber at Westminster, fulfilling a prophecy that he would die in Jerusalem.

items.name: Henry V
facts: Son of Henry IV; as a prince he was hit in the face by an arrow at Shrewsbury in 1403 and survived.
Crushed a Lollard rising led by his old friend Sir John Oldcastle in 1414.
Renewed the Hundred Years' War and captured Harfleur in 1415.
Won the Battle of Agincourt on 25 October 1415, St Crispin's Day, against a far larger French army.
Conquered Normandy between 1417 and 1419, taking Rouen after a long siege.
The Treaty of Troyes in 1420 made him heir to the French throne and he married Catherine of Valois.
Died of dysentery at Vincennes on 31 August 1422, aged 35, before he could become King of France.
Succeeded by his nine-month-old son Henry VI.

items.name: Henry VI
facts: Became king at nine months old; his uncles Bedford and Gloucester governed for him.
Crowned King of France in Paris in 1431, but Joan of Arc had already turned the war.
By 1453 England had lost all its French lands except Calais.
Founded Eton College in 1440 and King's College, Cambridge, in 1441.
Married the strong-willed Margaret of Anjou in 1445.
Suffered a mental breakdown in 1453, and Richard, Duke of York, was made Protector.
The Wars of the Roses began at the first Battle of St Albans on 22 May 1455.
Deposed by Edward IV in March 1461 and fled to Scotland; captured in 1465 and held in the Tower.

items.name: Edward IV
facts: Son of Richard, Duke of York, who was killed at Wakefield in December 1460.
Very tall and handsome in youth, over six feet three; a fine soldier who never lost a battle.
Won the Battle of Towton on 29 March 1461, the bloodiest battle fought on English soil.
Secretly married the widow Elizabeth Woodville in 1464, angering Warwick the Kingmaker.
Warwick captured him briefly in 1469 after the Battle of Edgecote, but had to release him.
Warwick and Edward's brother Clarence rebelled again, and Edward fled to Burgundy in October 1470.

items.name: Henry VI
facts: Restored in October 1470 by Warwick the Kingmaker, who had switched sides and allied with Margaret of Anjou; this is called the Readeption.
Henry was a feeble figurehead, paraded through London; Warwick and Clarence held the real power.
Edward IV returned from Burgundy in March 1471 and killed Warwick at the Battle of Barnet on 14 April.
Margaret's army was crushed at Tewkesbury on 4 May 1471 and Henry's only son, Prince Edward, was killed.
Killed in the Tower of London on 21 May 1471, probably on Edward IV's orders, ending the House of Lancaster.

items.name: Edward IV
facts: Returned from Burgundy in March 1471, landing at Ravenspur in Yorkshire with a small force.
Killed Warwick at Barnet on 14 April 1471 and crushed the Lancastrians at Tewkesbury on 4 May.
Invaded France in 1475 but took a French pension at Picquigny; the next year Caxton set up England's first printing press under his patronage.
Had his brother Clarence executed in 1478; legend says he was drowned in a butt of Malmsey wine.
His later reign was quiet and prosperous, but he grew fat and died suddenly on 9 April 1483, aged 40.

items.name: Edward V
facts: Son of Edward IV and Elizabeth Woodville; became king aged 12 on 9 April 1483.
His uncle Richard, Duke of Gloucester, seized him at Stony Stratford and arrested his Woodville relatives.
Lodged in the Tower of London with his younger brother Richard: the 'Princes in the Tower'.
Declared illegitimate in June 1483 on the grounds that his parents' marriage was invalid.
Reigned for about eleven weeks and was never crowned.
The princes disappeared in the summer of 1483 and are presumed to have been murdered.
Bones found in the Tower in 1674 were placed in Westminster Abbey as the princes.

items.name: Richard III
facts: Youngest brother of Edward IV; as Duke of Gloucester he fought loyally for Edward at Barnet and Tewkesbury.
Made Protector for his nephew Edward V in April 1483; took the throne on 26 June and was crowned on 6 July.
Had Lord Hastings executed without trial on 13 June 1483.
Widely suspected of murdering the Princes in the Tower.
Crushed the Duke of Buckingham's rebellion in October 1483.
His only son died in 1484 and his wife Anne Neville in March 1485.
Killed at the Battle of Bosworth on 22 August 1485 by the army of Henry Tudor.
The last English king to die in battle and the last Plantagenet king.
His skeleton was found under a Leicester car park in 2012 and reburied in Leicester Cathedral in 2015.

items.name: Henry VII
facts: Won the crown by defeating Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485.
Married Elizabeth of York in 1486, uniting the houses of Lancaster and York.
The red and white Tudor rose symbolised that union and the end of the Wars of the Roses.
Defeated the pretender Lambert Simnel at the Battle of Stoke Field in 1487.
Had the pretender Perkin Warbeck executed in 1499.
Built up a full royal treasury through careful finance and heavy fines on the nobles.
His elder son Arthur married Catherine of Aragon in 1501 but died in 1502.
Died in 1509 and was succeeded by his second son, Henry VIII.

items.name: Henry VIII
facts: Had six wives: Catherine of Aragon, Anne Boleyn, Jane Seymour, Anne of Cleves, Catherine Howard and Catherine Parr.
The rhyme for their fates: divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived.
Broke with Rome; the Act of Supremacy of 1534 made him head of the Church of England.
Dissolved the monasteries between 1536 and 1541, with Thomas Cromwell running the process.
Met Francis I of France at the Field of the Cloth of Gold in 1520.
Had Thomas More executed in 1535 and Thomas Cromwell executed in 1540.
His warship the Mary Rose sank in the Solent in 1545.
Died in 1547, leaving three children: Mary, Elizabeth and his successor Edward VI.

items.name: Edward VI
facts: Son of Henry VIII and Jane Seymour; became king aged nine in 1547.
Ruled first through his uncle Edward Seymour, Duke of Somerset, then through John Dudley, Duke of Northumberland.
The English won the Battle of Pinkie against Scotland in 1547.
The Act of Uniformity of 1549 introduced Thomas Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer; a second version followed in 1552.
Kett's Rebellion in Norfolk and the Prayer Book Rebellion in the West both broke out in 1549.
Somerset was executed in 1552.
Died aged 15 in 1553, probably of tuberculosis, having named Lady Jane Grey as his heir.

items.name: Lady Jane Grey
facts: Great-granddaughter of Henry VII; married Guildford Dudley, son of the Duke of Northumberland, in 1553.
Proclaimed queen on 10 July 1553, as Northumberland tried to keep Mary off the throne.
Deposed after nine days when the country rallied to Mary; called the Nine Days' Queen.
Beheaded at the Tower of London in February 1554, aged about 16.

items.name: Mary I
facts: Daughter of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon; the first queen to rule England in her own right.
Restored Roman Catholicism and the authority of the Pope.
Married Philip II of Spain at Winchester Cathedral in 1554; they had no children.
Wyatt's Rebellion against the Spanish marriage was crushed in 1554.
Had around 280 Protestants burned at the stake, including Cranmer, Latimer and Ridley.
Her burnings earned her the nickname Bloody Mary.
Lost Calais, England's last possession in France, in 1558.
Died in 1558 and was succeeded by her half-sister Elizabeth.

items.name: Elizabeth I
facts: Daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn; became queen in 1558 aged 25.
Her Religious Settlement of 1559 re-established the Protestant Church of England.
Never married and was known as the Virgin Queen; Virginia was named after her.
Had Mary, Queen of Scots, executed at Fotheringhay in 1587 after the Babington Plot.
The Spanish Armada was defeated in 1588; she rallied the troops at Tilbury.
Francis Drake sailed round the world between 1577 and 1580 and was knighted in 1581.
Her reign was the age of Shakespeare and Marlowe; the Poor Law was passed in 1601.
Died in 1603 and was succeeded by James VI of Scotland, ending the Tudor line.

items.name: James I
facts: Already James VI of Scotland since 1567; his accession in 1603 was the Union of the Crowns.
Son of Mary, Queen of Scots; married Anne of Denmark.
The Gunpowder Plot to blow up Parliament was foiled on 5 November 1605; Guy Fawkes was caught.
Jamestown, Virginia, England's first permanent colony in America, was founded in 1607.
The King James Bible, the Authorised Version, was published in 1611.
The Pilgrim Fathers sailed to America on the Mayflower in 1620.
Believed in the divine right of kings and quarrelled with Parliament over money.
Died in 1625 and was succeeded by his son Charles I, his elder son Henry having died in 1612.

items.name: Charles I
facts: Married Henrietta Maria of France, a Catholic, in 1625.
Accepted the Petition of Right in 1628 but ruled without Parliament from 1629 to 1640.
Raised money without Parliament through Ship Money.
The Bishops' Wars with Scotland forced him to recall Parliament in 1640.
Tried and failed to arrest five MPs in the Commons in January 1642.
The Civil War began at Edgehill in 1642; he lost at Marston Moor in 1644 and Naseby in 1645.
His advisers Strafford and Archbishop Laud were executed in 1641 and 1645.
Tried for treason and beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall on 30 January 1649.

items.name: Oliver Cromwell (Lord Protector)
facts: After Charles I's execution in 1649, England was a republic, the Commonwealth, ruled by Parliament until 1653.
Cromwell was a cavalry commander in the New Model Army, which beat the Royalists at Naseby in 1645.
Led a brutal campaign in Ireland in 1649, including the storming of Drogheda and Wexford.
Beat the Scots at Dunbar in 1650 and Charles II's army at Worcester in 1651.
Dissolved the Rump Parliament in 1653 and became Lord Protector in December 1653.
Ruled through the Major-Generals from 1655 to 1657 and allowed Jews back into England in 1656.
Refused the offer of the crown in 1657.
Died on 3 September 1658; after the Restoration his body was dug up and hanged at Tyburn in 1661.

items.name: Richard Cromwell (Lord Protector)
facts: Oliver Cromwell's son; became Lord Protector on his father's death in September 1658.
Lacked the support of the army and was nicknamed Tumbledown Dick.
Resigned in May 1659 and the Rump Parliament was recalled; the monarchy was restored in 1660.
Lived quietly abroad and then in England, dying in 1712 aged 85.

items.name: Charles II
facts: Hid in an oak tree at Boscobel after losing the Battle of Worcester in 1651.
Restored to the throne in 1660 with General Monck's help, entering London on 29 May, his 30th birthday.
Married Catherine of Braganza in 1662; many mistresses, including Nell Gwyn, but no legitimate children.
The Great Plague struck London in 1665 and the Great Fire in 1666.
The Dutch raided the Medway and burned English ships in 1667.
The Habeas Corpus Act was passed in 1679.
The Popish Plot of 1678 and the Exclusion Crisis gave rise to the names Whig and Tory.
Known as the Merry Monarch; died in 1685 and was succeeded by his brother James.

items.name: James II
facts: Catholic younger brother of Charles II; also James VII of Scotland.
Crushed the Monmouth Rebellion at Sedgemoor in 1685; Judge Jeffreys then held the Bloody Assizes.
His Declaration of Indulgence of 1687 suspended laws against Catholics and Dissenters.
Seven bishops who opposed him were tried and acquitted in June 1688.
The birth of his Catholic son in June 1688 raised fears of a Catholic dynasty.
William of Orange landed at Torbay in November 1688 and James fled to France: the Glorious Revolution.
Defeated at the Battle of the Boyne in Ireland in 1690.
Died in exile in France in 1701; his son became the Old Pretender.

items.name: William III and Mary II
facts: Mary was James II's Protestant daughter; William was her Dutch husband and James's nephew.
Offered the crown jointly by Parliament in 1689 and accepted the Bill of Rights.
The Toleration Act of 1689 gave freedom of worship to Protestant Dissenters.
William defeated James II at the Battle of the Boyne on 1 July 1690.
The Massacre of Glencoe took place in 1692.
The Bank of England was founded in 1694; Mary died of smallpox the same year, childless.
The Act of Settlement of 1701 passed the succession to the Protestant House of Hanover.
William died in 1702 after his horse stumbled on a molehill; his sister-in-law Anne succeeded.

items.name: Anne
facts: Younger daughter of James II; married Prince George of Denmark in 1683.
Had seventeen pregnancies but no surviving child; her son William died in 1700 aged 11.
The Duke of Marlborough won Blenheim in 1704, Ramillies in 1706, Oudenarde in 1708 and Malplaquet in 1709.
Gibraltar was captured in 1704.
The Act of Union with Scotland in 1707 created the Kingdom of Great Britain.
Her close friend Sarah Churchill, Duchess of Marlborough, was replaced in her favour by Abigail Masham.
The Treaty of Utrecht ended the War of the Spanish Succession in 1713.
Died in 1714, the last Stuart monarch; George of Hanover succeeded under the Act of Settlement.

items.name: George I
facts: Elector of Hanover and great-grandson of James I; more than fifty Catholics with better claims were passed over.
Born in Germany and spoke mainly German and French, not English.
Had his wife Sophia Dorothea locked up in Ahlden Castle from 1694 until her death in 1726.
The Jacobite rising of 1715, the Fifteen, was defeated.
The South Sea Bubble burst in 1720, ruining many investors.
Robert Walpole took charge of the government from 1721, becoming the first Prime Minister.
The Septennial Act of 1716 allowed Parliaments to last seven years.
Died in 1727 at Osnabruck on the way to Hanover; succeeded by his son George II.

items.name: George II
facts: Born in Hanover, the last British monarch born outside Great Britain.
Handel wrote Zadok the Priest for his coronation in 1727.
Married Caroline of Ansbach, who died in 1737.
Led his troops at Dettingen in 1743, the last British monarch to fight in battle.
The Jacobite rising of 1745 under Bonnie Prince Charlie ended at Culloden in 1746.
Britain switched to the Gregorian calendar in 1752, losing eleven days.
The Seven Years' War began in 1756; Wolfe took Quebec in 1759, the Year of Victories.
His son Frederick died in 1751, so his grandson George III succeeded him in 1760.

items.name: George III
facts: First Hanoverian king born in Britain, with English as his first language.
Married Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz in 1761 and had fifteen children.
Bought Buckingham House in 1761; it later became Buckingham Palace.
Lost the American colonies in the War of Independence, 1775 to 1783.
The Act of Union with Ireland in 1801 created the United Kingdom.
Britain fought Revolutionary and Napoleonic France; Trafalgar in 1805, Waterloo in 1815.
Parliament abolished the slave trade in 1807.
Nicknamed Farmer George; bouts of madness led to the Regency of 1811 and he died in 1820.

items.name: George IV
facts: Ruled as Prince Regent from 1811 to 1820 during his father's illness, giving the Regency era its name.
Secretly and unlawfully married Maria Fitzherbert in 1785, then Caroline of Brunswick in 1795.
His only child, Princess Charlotte, died in childbirth in 1817.
Tried to divorce Caroline in 1820 and had her barred from his coronation in 1821.
Built the Royal Pavilion at Brighton and employed John Nash on Regent Street and Buckingham Palace.
Visited Scotland in 1822 wearing a kilt, the first reigning monarch there since the 1650s.
Reluctantly agreed to Catholic Emancipation in 1829 under Wellington.
Nicknamed Prinny; fat and debt-ridden, he died in 1830 and his brother William succeeded.

items.name: William IV
facts: Joined the Royal Navy at 13 and was a friend of Nelson; known as the Sailor King.
Had ten illegitimate children with the actress Dorothea Jordan.
Married Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen in 1818; their two daughters died in infancy.
The Great Reform Act of 1832 passed under Earl Grey after William agreed to create new peers.
The Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 ended slavery across most of the British Empire.
The Factory Act of 1833 and the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834 were passed.
The old Palace of Westminster burned down in 1834.
Died in 1837; his niece Victoria succeeded, and Hanover passed to his brother Ernest.

items.name: Victoria
facts: Became queen in 1837 aged 18; her father, the Duke of Kent, had died in 1820.
Married Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha in 1840; they had nine children.
Albert organised the Great Exhibition at the Crystal Palace in 1851.
The Crimean War, 1854 to 1856, led to the Victoria Cross in 1856.
Albert died in 1861 and she wore black for the rest of her life.
Disraeli made her Empress of India in 1876; her other Prime Ministers included Peel, Palmerston and Gladstone.
Celebrated her Golden Jubilee in 1887 and Diamond Jubilee in 1897.
Died in January 1901 at Osborne House after 63 years; succeeded by her son Edward VII.

items.name: Edward VII
facts: Known as Bertie; waited nearly sixty years as Prince of Wales before becoming king aged 59.
Married Alexandra of Denmark in 1863; they had six children.
Took the house name Saxe-Coburg and Gotha from his father, Prince Albert.
Had many mistresses and was caught up in the Tranby Croft baccarat scandal of 1891.
His coronation was postponed in 1902 when he needed an operation for appendicitis.
The Entente Cordiale with France was signed in 1904; he was called the Peacemaker.
The Liberals won a landslide in 1906; Lloyd George's People's Budget of 1909 caused a crisis with the Lords.
Died in 1910 and was succeeded by his son George V.

items.name: George V
facts: A naval officer and second son; became heir when his brother Albert Victor died in 1892.
Married Mary of Teck in 1893; she had been engaged to his late brother.
The Parliament Act of 1911 cut the power of the House of Lords.
Reigned through the First World War, 1914 to 1918.
Changed the royal family's name from Saxe-Coburg and Gotha to Windsor in 1917.
The Irish Free State was created in 1922; the first Labour government took office in 1924.
The General Strike was in 1926; he gave the first royal Christmas radio broadcast in 1932.
Celebrated his Silver Jubilee in 1935 and died at Sandringham in January 1936.

items.name: Edward VIII
facts: Reigned from 20 January to 11 December 1936 and was never crowned.
Abdicated to marry the American divorcee Wallis Simpson, which Prime Minister Baldwin opposed.
Became Duke of Windsor and married Wallis in France in June 1937.
Governor of the Bahamas from 1940 to 1945; died in Paris in 1972.

items.name: George VI
facts: Born Albert and known as Bertie; became king when his brother abdicated in 1936.
Fought at the Battle of Jutland in 1916 as a naval officer.
Married Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon in 1923; their daughters were Elizabeth and Margaret.
Had a stammer and was helped by the speech therapist Lionel Logue.
Stayed in London during the Blitz; Buckingham Palace was bombed in 1940.
Reigned through the Second World War with Churchill as Prime Minister from 1940.
Was the last Emperor of India; India became independent in 1947.
Died at Sandringham in February 1952 and was succeeded by his daughter Elizabeth II.

items.name: Elizabeth II
facts: Served as a driver and mechanic in the ATS during the Second World War.
Married Philip Mountbatten in 1947; children Charles, Anne, Andrew and Edward.
Became queen in February 1952 while in Kenya; her coronation was televised on 2 June 1953.
Her first Prime Minister was Churchill and her last was Liz Truss, fifteen in all.
Called 1992 her annus horribilis after the Windsor Castle fire and family break-ups.
Diana, Princess of Wales, died in 1997.
Celebrated Silver, Golden, Diamond and Platinum Jubilees in 1977, 2002, 2012 and 2022.
Died at Balmoral on 8 September 2022 after 70 years, the longest reign in British history.

items.name: Charles III
facts: Born in 1948; Prince of Wales from 1958 and the longest-serving heir apparent.
Served in the Royal Navy and RAF from 1971 to 1976 and founded the Prince's Trust in 1976.
Married Lady Diana Spencer in 1981; sons William and Harry; divorced in 1996.
Married Camilla Parker Bowles in 2005.
Became king on 8 September 2022 aged 73, the oldest person to take the throne.
Crowned with Queen Camilla at Westminster Abbey on 6 May 2023.
Long known for campaigning on the environment and organic farming at Highgrove.
Announced in February 2024 that he was being treated for cancer.
